query: For high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could improve hardness and strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to produce the improvement, a measurable outcome relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with clear observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment to a eutectic high-entropy alloy (specifically Al0.7CoCrFeNi) will simultaneously increase its hardness/strength and tensile ductility by inducing a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, thereby overcoming the conventional strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized eutectic high-entropy alloy Al0.7CoCrFeNi (composition: Al 14.8, Co 21.3, Cr 21.3, Fe 21.3, Ni 21.3 at.%) with a dual-phase lamellae microstructure consisting of alternating FCC and BCC (B2 ordered) phases separated by incoherent interfaces with a ~10 nm transition layer. Initial state is strong but brittle with low ductility.
generation.intervention: High-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment at 6 GPa and 1473 K.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; treatment applied to the specific eutectic HEA composition Al0.7CoCrFeNi; pressure and temperature must be sufficient to induce microstructural reorganization without phase transformation (XRD confirms phase constitution remains FCC+BCC).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure composed of hexagonal-like structural units interconnected by FCC phase, with coherent FCC/B2 interfaces (mismatch factor ~0.004) and absence of incoherent transition layers.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces and hierarchical pattern promote multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, deformation twins) at multiple length scales, relieve stress concentration at interfaces, and arrest interfacial cracking. This leads to delocalized damage accumulation and prevents crack coalescence, enhancing both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ultimate tensile strength will increase by approximately 100% (from ~575 MPa to ~1150 MPa) and tensile ductility will increase by approximately 100% (from ~18% to ~36%) compared to the untreated baseline, while maintaining structural integrity.
generation.baseline: Untreated homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy with dual-phase lamellae and incoherent interfaces, exhibiting high strength but brittle failure with low ductility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is specific to eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellae structures amenable to HPHT-induced hierarchical patterning. Generalizability to other HEA systems (e.g., refractory HEAs, single-phase FCC HEAs) is not confirmed. The effect is dependent on achieving the specific coherent interface structure; conventional hot isostatic pressing or thermal-mechanical treatments without high pressure do not produce the same result.
generation.uncertainty: The mechanism relies on the specific formation of coherent interfaces and hierarchical patterns which may not occur in all HEA compositions or processing conditions. The long-term stability of the hierarchically patterned microstructure under cyclic loading or extreme environments is not fully characterized. The exact pressure-temperature window for optimal results may vary by alloy system.
generation.falsification_experiment: Apply HPHT treatment (6 GPa, 1473 K) to the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy and perform tensile testing. Falsification occurs if: (1) the strength does not increase by at least 50% relative to the baseline, OR (2) the ductility does not increase by at least 50% relative to the baseline, OR (3) the microstructure fails to develop a hierarchically patterned structure with coherent FCC/B2 interfaces (verified by TEM/EBSD), OR (4) the material exhibits brittle failure with ductility <10% after treatment. Additionally, if conventional hot isostatic pressing (without high pressure) produces similar results, the specific role of high pressure would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

We used the homogenized Al 0.7 CoCrFeNi (molar ratio) alloy [18] (hereafter termed Ho alloy) with a composition of Al 14.8 Co 21.3 Cr 21.3 Fe 21.3 Ni 21.3 (at. %) and the typical dual-phase lamellae microstructure (Fig. 1a, b ) as the precursor material for HPHT treatment. The corresponding EBSD phase map (Fig. 1c ) clearly reveals the dual-phase lamellae consisting of alternating face-centered cubic (FCC) layers and body-centered cubic (BCC) layers. After HPHT treatment (Fig. 1f ) at a pressure of 6 GPa and a temperature of 1473 K (more details see Methods), we confirmed that there is no change in the phase constitutions with X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Fig. 1g ), where the corresponding peak positions of the HPHT-treated alloy are shifted slightly rightward due to densification. Notably, the HPHT-treated alloy exhibits a hierarchically patterned microstructure (Fig. 1h ) consisting of hexagonal-like structural units (Fig. 1i ). The corresponding EBSD phase map (Fig. 1j ) reveals that the interior of each structural unit is composed of a mixture of FCC and BCC phases, while different units are interconnected by the FCC phase.
